abstract_text:
Abstract
The fundamental challenge in modeling thermally induced deformations in advanced manufacturing lies in resolving the trade-off between black-box data-driven approaches and physical interpretability. While high predictive accuracy is essential, stringent transparency is equally required to ensure industrial reliability. To bridge this critical gap, this paper introduces a generalized, physics-informed interpretable modeling framework driven by the Dynamic Temporal Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (DT-KAN). We apply this methodology to the characterization, prediction, and real-time compensation of six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) thermal errors in precision CNC machine tools. These errors remain a persistent challenge in novel coaxial dual-lead feed drive systems due to complex macro–micro thermo-mechanical coupling. The proposed DT-KAN synergizes explicit physics-based temporal feature engineering with a learnable activation function architecture. Unlike standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), the network replaces fixed weights with learnable B-splines on its edges. This structural shift enables the autonomous extraction of high-fidelity functional mappings while preserving the physical inductive biases associated with thermal superposition. Under rigorous cross-validation with unseen operating conditions, the DT-KAN achieved a coefficient of determination (𝑅2
) of 0.958 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.91 μ
rad, significantly outperforming benchmark models in both accuracy and parameter efficiency. Beyond exceptional predictive performance, the model offers superior interpretability by autonomously decoupling underlying physical mechanisms. It explicitly identifies cumulative heat as the driver of thermal memory, and thermal gradients as the source of dynamic hysteresis. Finally, the industrial viability of the framework was validated through a closed-loop, real-time compensation system on a dual-drive grinding center. The proposed method reduced the maximum volumetric error from 31.6 μ
m to 5.2 μ
m (an 83.5% improvement), effectively restoring the system to its cold-state accuracy. Practical precision grinding trials of linear guide sliders further confirmed that this approach ensures process stability and zero-defect rates under thermally unstable conditions. These findings highlight the immense potential of interpretable modeling as a pathway to transparent and reliable thermal error compensation in modern manufacturing.

    - heading "Introduction" [level=2]
    - generic: In contemporary manufacturing, the machining accuracy of machine tools fundamentally governs product reliability and functional integrity [1]. However, achieving sub-micron precision is persistently challenged by various error sources. Among these factors, thermal errors originating from the coupling of various internal heat sources, exemplified by spindle bearings [2], servo motors [3], and ballscrew friction [4], with fluctuating ambient temperatures [5], are widely recognized as the primary contributors to machining inaccuracies. A substantial academic literature and industrial metrology data consistently attribute 40% to 75% of the total machining error budget of a machine tool to thermal phenomena [6]. This statistic underscores a critical imperative. The development of a comprehensive scientific framework to holistically address the thermal error problem, ranging from its fundamental generation to high-fidelity prediction and effective real-time compensation, represents a strategic frontier for advancing high-performance manufacturing systems [7], [8].
    - text: "This research focuses on the complex feed systems that constitute the kinematic core of modern multi-axis machine tools [9]. Within these sophisticated assemblies, the generation mechanism of thermal error transcends the classical one-dimensional elongation model. The intricate interplay of multiple, distributed heat sources with complex structural loops and kinematic constraints gives rise to a far more challenging scenario [10]. The non-uniform temperature fields and dynamic heat fluxes propagating through the machine structure do not merely cause linear expansion along an axis of motion. Instead, they induce complex thermomechanical responses, including structural bending and torsional warping, which manifest as a spatially and temporally evolving error field. This field is most accurately described in its full dimensionality: a six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) error vector at the Tool Center Point (TCP), comprising three translational components ("

    - text: ) [11], [12]. Crucially, angular errors exert a disproportionate impact on volumetric accuracy. Through Abbe and sine error mechanisms [13], micro-radian scale thermal rotations are amplified into substantial positional discrepancies at the cutting interface, particularly within large working envelopes. Crucially, these six error components are not independent variables. They are intricately coupled through the underlying thermo-structural dynamics, exhibiting strong cross-axis dependencies, pronounced nonlinearity, and significant temporal hysteresis (the “thermal memory” effect). A profound lack of deep, quantitative characterization of this complex 6-DOF thermal error generation process represents the first critical gap in the current body of knowledge, fundamentally limiting the efficacy of any subsequent modeling and control strategies.
    - generic: "To address this challenge, existing research has divided into two primary avenues for error prediction: physics-based and data-driven modeling, both of which encounter significant bottlenecks when confronted with the 6-DOF problem. The first-principles approach, typified by the Finite Element Method (FEM), offers valuable physical insight into thermo-structural behavior and is an indispensable tool during the machine design phase for optimizing thermal stability [6], [14]. However, its application to real-time error compensation is fundamentally hindered by practical barriers. Firstly, the construction of a high-fidelity FEM model demands an exhaustive and often unattainable level of detail regarding geometric intricacies, material thermal properties, and, most critically, the precise characterization of boundary conditions like contact thermal resistance and convective heat transfer coefficients, which are notoriously difficult to measure and are themselves dynamically variable. Secondly, the immense computational expense associated with solving the coupled partial differential equations of thermo-elasticity renders FEM far too slow for the millisecond-level prediction cycles required for online control [15]."
    - generic: These inherent limitations have catalyzed a decisive shift in research focus toward data-driven approaches [16]. This methodology circumvents the need for explicit physical formulation by directly learning the complex mapping between measurable inputs, typically a distributed network of temperature sensors, and the resulting 6-DOF thermal error outputs. The evolution of this field reflects a growing recognition of the problem’s inherent complexity. Early approaches such as Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) often failed to capture the strong nonlinearities and temporal dynamics involved [17], [18]. A significant step forward was later marked by the adoption of more advanced machine learning architectures, including widely used Backpropagation Neural Networks (BPNN) [19], [20], Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for spatial feature extraction, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for modeling temporal dependencies [21], [22]. However, a critical interpretability gap remains. While state-of-the-art hybrid models such as CNN-LSTM [23], [24] achieve high accuracy, they function as opaque systems that obscure the causal chain between thermal stimuli and geometric deformation. Their reliance on the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with fixed node-based activation functions obscures the internal mapping mechanism. Consequently, researchers cannot derive explicit expressions describing the error evolution or verify whether the network’s parameters correspond to actual physical changes rather than numerical noise. This lack of interpretability isolates the learning process from physical reality, leading to performance degradation under unseen conditions [25], [26].
    - generic: Furthermore, a critical disconnect exists between theoretical prediction and effective compensation. Even if a high-fidelity 6-DOF prediction model were available, most current industrial control systems are limited to compensating for only one-dimensional or, at best, three-dimensional translational errors. The technical infrastructure and kinematic algorithms required to dynamically modulate the machine’s axes to counteract all six degrees of freedom in real time are exceptionally challenging to implement and are rarely reported in practice [27], [28]. This disconnect ultimately hinders the translation of advanced modeling into tangible improvements in manufacturing precision.
    - generic: "While the aforementioned literature demonstrates the undeniable predictive prowess of advanced neural architectures, a critical scientific gap persists: the accuracy-interpretability dilemma (as conceptualized in Fig. 1). Existing data-driven methodologies lack the intrinsic structural capacity to autonomously extract and mathematically articulate fundamental thermodynamic mechanisms from sensory data. Functioning primarily as black-box observational instruments, they fit data effectively but fail to isolate the underlying physical phenomena. Consequently, they are largely relegated to bespoke statistical fitting exercises rather than serving as generic scientific tools for physical insight. The fundamental academic challenge in modern thermal error research is therefore not merely achieving higher predictive accuracy, but breaking the current Pareto frontier that forces a trade-off between performance and structural transparency. The core objective is to autonomously decouple fundamental thermodynamic mechanisms, such as cumulative thermal memory and non-linear hysteresis, directly from complex, entangled multi-sensor data."
    - generic: To systematically address this industry-critical gap, this paper proposes a generic and inherently interpretable modeling framework for the comprehensive management of 6-DOF thermal errors. We utilize a novel coaxial dual-lead feed drive system as a rigorous scientific testbed. This “dual-source, shared-structure” architecture creates an exceptionally severe macro–micro thermo-mechanical coupling environment, providing ideal conditions to elicit and observe complex nonlinear error dynamics. Following the initial empirical characterization of this dual-drive system, we deploy the proposed Dynamic Temporal Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (DT-KAN). In contrast to traditional networks, the KAN architecture [29], [30] replaces fixed weights with learnable B-spline activation functions on its edges. A key distinction of our approach is the departure from Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which rely on opaque hidden states to model memory. Instead, the proposed DT-KAN employs explicit physics-based temporal feature engineering, ensuring that critical dynamics, such as thermal inertia, are preserved in a transparent input space. Through these physics-aligned inductive biases, the DT-KAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while autonomously deriving human-readable symbolic formulas that align with physically plausible functional relationships. Finally, a real-time compensation algorithm compatible with modern CNC infrastructures is designed and validated, thus closing the loop from intelligent modeling to demonstrable industrial impact.
